At nine, Zeenat stood up in class to read about volcanoes and stumbled on "eruption". Before anyone could snicker, she puffed her cheeks, made a rumbling noise and pretended to explode all over her desk. The class shrieked with laughter. Her teacher Hemant hid a smile, and Zeenat sat down grinning, though her hands were still cold.

At fifteen, Zeenat's feed was full of memes she edited herself: cats in exam halls, a cartoon of herself asleep on a pile of books, captions like "me, thriving 🙂". People commented, "You're the funniest person ever." She posted every night, choosing which photos to keep and cropping out her messy desk.

One afternoon her friend Samir sat beside her on the steps. "Your posts are brilliant," he said. "But you haven't said anything real in weeks. How are you actually doing with the exams?" Zeenat looked at her phone, then at the ground. "Honestly? I'm scared I'll fail," she said quietly.

qa.q: What did Zeenat pretend to do when she stumbled on the word eruption?
qa.a: She puffed her cheeks, made a rumbling noise and pretended to explode all over her desk.

qa.q: How is Zeenat's joke in class at nine like the memes she posts at fifteen?
qa.a: At nine Zeenat puffs her cheeks and explodes over her desk after stumbling; at fifteen she edits memes, crops out her messy desk and posts "me, thriving". Both times she shows a funny, chosen self, while her cold hands and her scared answer to Samir show something more.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling as she sat down grinning with cold hands?
qa.a: Zeenat was still nervous and embarrassed under the grin, even though the joke had worked.

qa.q: What did Samir do that opened the way for Zeenat to speak honestly?
qa.a: Samir praised her posts, then asked in person how she was actually doing with the exams, which gave her a safe moment to say she was scared.

grounding: Humour that covers embarrassment in a child, and a teenager's curated memes and photos as a presented self that hides real worry.

At nine, Simran stumbled while reading about the water cycle and ended up with the word "evaporation" in a knot. She crossed her eyes and made a hissing kettle noise. The class roared and the teacher, Yamini, sighed with a laugh. Simran bowed, then sat still, biting her thumbnail.

At fifteen, in the corridor, Simran gave her friend Jomon a mock salute. "Captain of the lost-and-found," she said, because he had found her missing lunchbox. Jomon saluted back, grinning. A minute later another boy passed and said to Jomon, with a flat voice and air quotes around the word, "Your 'project' was really something." Jomon's grin dropped and he looked at the floor.

Simran recognised that feeling. She stepped between them, said, "That wasn't funny, and you know it," and walked Jomon away. "Same gesture as mine," she said quietly on the stairs, "but not the same tone, was it?" Jomon breathed out and nodded.

qa.q: What noise did Simran make after crossing her eyes at nine?
qa.a: She made a hissing kettle noise.

qa.q: How do the two gestures at fifteen differ, and how does this link back to Simran's joke at nine?
qa.a: Simran's mock salute is friendly teasing that Jomon returns, while the boy's air quotes carry a put-down that makes Jomon look at the floor; the tone decides it, and Simran, who once used humour to cover her own embarrassment, recognises that feeling.

qa.q: What was Jomon probably feeling after the boy's remark about his project?
qa.a: Jomon felt hurt and embarrassed, so his grin disappeared and he looked at the floor.

qa.q: What did Simran do that helped Jomon?
qa.a: Simran told the boy the comment was not funny, walked Jomon away, and talked with him about how the same gesture can feel different with a different tone.

grounding: Humour as cover for embarrassment at nine, later recognised by the same person when air quotes and salutes read as friendly or as a put-down depending on tone.

passage:
At five, Abhinav pressed his face into his mother Reena's side at a family gathering, refusing to say hello to a cousin's friends. Reena did not push him. She put a hand on his shoulder, said, "I'm right here," and stayed near the balloons until he peeked out and took one.

At fifteen, after his grandfather died suddenly, Abhinav took every framed photograph off his shelf and slid them into a drawer. When anyone said his grandfather's name, he left the room. His sister Afreen tried to share a memory at dinner and he pushed his plate away. The house felt quieter each day, and the hurt did not fade; it flared every time someone said his grandfather's name by accident.

One evening Reena left the family album on the sofa and sat near the door, saying only, "I'm here when you're ready." An hour later Abhinav sat beside her, opened the album to the last page and said, "I miss him." Afreen came in and sat on his other side.

qa.q: What did Abhinav take from Reena's side at the gathering at five?
qa.a: He took a balloon after peeking out from beside her.

qa.q: How is Abhinav's avoidance at five like his avoidance at fifteen, and what helped both times?
qa.a: At five Abhinav presses his face into his mother's side and Reena stays near until he peeks out; at fifteen he slides the photographs into a drawer and leaves the room at his grandfather's name, and Reena again sits near the door until he comes to her. Avoiding feels like relief but the hurt flares, and gentle nearness helps.

qa.q: What might Abhinav be feeling as he pushes his plate away when Afreen shares a memory?
qa.a: Abhinav is in deep pain and afraid of hurting more, so he avoids reminders of his grandfather.

qa.q: What did Reena do that helped Abhinav open up?
qa.a: Reena left the album where he could find it, sat near, and told him she was there when he was ready, rather than forcing him to talk.

grounding: Avoidance in a young child hiding behind a parent, and a bereaved teenager avoiding reminders, with gentle nearness helping in both.

At nine, Sarika dropped her book while reading aloud and the class went silent. She made a big show of tripping over her own shoes, did a wobbly bow and kept the room laughing until the teacher said, "Thank you, Sarika, sit down." Only when she sat did she wipe her damp hands on her skirt.

At fifteen, at the tea stall after school, Sarika said with an absolutely blank face, "Suraj, your haircut makes you look like a tired coconut." Suraj froze. Was that humour, or a dig? Nobody laughed. Sarika, usually the loudest in the group, kept her expression flat and waited.

Ishita, standing beside them, asked, "Wait, was that meant to be funny?" Sarika blinked. "Yes! It's a good haircut. I like coconuts." Suraj let out a breath and grinned. "You could've told me with a smile." Sarika laughed. "Fair. Next time I'll wink, I promise."

qa.q: What did Sarika call Suraj's haircut at the tea stall?
qa.a: She said it made him look like a tired coconut.

qa.q: What do Sarika's jokes at nine and fifteen have in common, and how do they differ?
qa.a: Both are jokes that keep control of a moment, the silly bow after the dropped book and the deadpan haircut remark, but the first clearly shows comedy while the blank face at fifteen leaves listeners unsure, so Ishita has to ask.

qa.q: What was Suraj probably feeling when Sarika said his haircut looked like a tired coconut?
qa.a: Suraj felt unsure and a little hurt, since he could not tell whether Sarika was joking.

qa.q: What did Ishita do that settled the confusion?
qa.a: Ishita simply asked whether the remark was meant to be funny, which let Sarika explain and Suraj relax.

grounding: Humour used to keep control of an embarrassing moment in childhood, and later a deadpan joke that others cannot tell from an insult until someone asks.

At ten, Seema and her friend Hafsa argued over one swing. Seema said, "You pick this game today, I pick tomorrow." Hafsa agreed, and they wrote the plan on the wall of the sandpit with a stick so they would remember. It worked for the whole term.

At fifteen, Seema told her older brother Madhav that Hafsa was the best friend anyone could wish for. Two days later Hafsa cancelled a shopping trip to help a cousin, and Seema stormed into the kitchen. "She is a complete fraud. I never want to see her again." Madhav stirred his tea and asked, "Was it only that, or is there more?" Seema opened her mouth, closed it and admitted, "She also sat with me every night last winter."

She thought of the sandpit and the wall, of listening to each side. That evening she texted Hafsa: "I was really cross. Can we sort it out, like when we did the swings?"

qa.q: What did Seema and Hafsa write on the wall of the sandpit?
qa.a: They wrote their plan for picking games in turn.

qa.q: How does Seema's approach to Hafsa at ten differ from her reaction at fifteen, and what brings the two together?
qa.a: At ten the two friends split turns so that each side feels heard, but at fifteen Seema swings from best friend to complete fraud over one cancelled trip; recalling the swing deal helps her hold the anger and the loyalty together and ask to sort it out.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when she called Hafsa a fraud?
qa.a: Seema felt hurt and angry about the cancelled trip, and the strong feeling made it hard to remember Hafsa's kindness.

qa.q: What did Madhav do that helped Seema?
qa.a: Madhav stayed calm, stirred his tea and asked whether there was more, which let Seema recall that Hafsa had also sat with her every night.

grounding: Splitting into all good and all bad in a teenager's friendship, and the earlier habit of compromise and turns that helps her hold both sides together.

After ten minutes of colouring, five-year-old Tanuja slumped against the sofa. "I'm bored. Can I watch something?" Her father Vijay handed her a shoebox of buttons and bottle caps and said, "See what these can become." She groaned. Then she lined the buttons up into a long train and announced that it was going to the moon.

The next morning at nursery, Tanuja wandered from the water table to the door and back, whining, "What can I do?" She dragged her feet by the shelves. Her teacher Gurleen did not scold her or hand her a screen. She knelt and said, "You can build with the blocks or paint with the big brush. Which one?" Tanuja thought for a moment, said, "Blocks," and started stacking them into a tower for her moon train.

By the time the tea break came, the tower was taller than she was, and she showed it to everyone.

qa.q: What did Vijay give Tanuja when she said she was bored?
qa.a: Vijay gave her a shoebox of buttons and bottle caps.

qa.q: How do Vijay at home and Gurleen at nursery handle the same boredom?
qa.a: Both give Tanuja something simple to work with rather than a screen or a scolding, a shoebox of buttons at home and a choice between blocks and paint at nursery, and in both cases her boredom turns into building.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling as she wandered and whined "What can I do?"
qa.a: Tanuja was restless and unengaged, with nothing holding her attention, and wanted someone to show her something to do.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that helped Tanuja settle?
qa.a: Gurleen knelt and offered two clear choices, blocks or the big brush, which let Tanuja decide and start.

grounding: Boredom in a preschooler at home and at nursery, each time met with simple materials or a small choice that lets imagination start.
